title: Barbara Liskov and the Substitution Principle (1987)
explainer: The 'L' in SOLID traces to a specific moment: computer scientist Barbara Liskov's 1987 OOPSLA keynote, 'Data Abstraction and Hierarchy,' where she first articulated the idea that a subtype should be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking the caller's assumptions. The precise, formal version of that requirement was worked out later, with Jeannette Wing, in a 1994 paper - so the principle used today is really the product of two passes, a conceptual one and a formal one, years apart. Liskov had already co-invented foundational ideas in data abstraction and distributed computing by the time of that keynote, work that later won her the 2008 ACM Turing Award.

title: Bertrand Meyer, Eiffel, and 'Open for Extension, Closed for Modification' (1988)
explainer: The 'O' in SOLID - open for extension, closed for modification - was coined by Bertrand Meyer in his 1988 book 'Object-Oriented Software Construction,' where it described a module stable enough that other code could depend on it (closed) while still allowing new behavior to be added (open). Meyer's own language, Eiffel, backed this with design-by-contract: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants checked whenever a class is used. Robert C. Martin later reframed the principle in 1996 around depending on abstractions rather than modifying concrete modules - the version usually taught today - and it was Michael Feathers, not Martin, who actually coined the 'SOLID' acronym bundling it with the other four principles.
